tagline.text: A palm-fringed southwest tip of Tablas Island with west-facing sunsets

location.label: Location
location.text: Southwestern tip of Tablas Island, Barangay Agmanic, Santa Fe, Romblon

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱650–2,000 (per person, from a day trip by scooter to one night in a bungalow)

children.text: Tablas Point is a quiet, palm-lined beach at the southwestern tip of Tablas Island in Santa Fe, Romblon. It opens to the west, so the sun sets over calm water, and the unpaved ride to get there is part of the appeal.

Tablas Point is a headland and beach at the southwestern end of Tablas, the largest island in Romblon province, on the Barangay Agmanic side of the municipality of Santa Fe. Wikipedia describes Santa Fe as a municipality on the southern tip of the island, with about 17,600 residents in the 2024 census. It can be reached by boat from the Caticlan side near Boracay, but it is not a crowded destination, and arriving feels like discovering a truly remote beach.

The heart of this place is the western sky. The beach faces due west, so you can watch the sun sink into the sea with nothing in the way, and travel bloggers describe the water as so still that the sky is mirrored on the surface. Rows of palms, boats pulled up on the sand, fishing nets and simple huts make natural photo backdrops. Beyond relaxing, playing volleyball and a shallow swim there is little else to do, which suits anyone who wants quiet rest.

The way in shapes the character of the trip. The last few kilometers are a rocky unpaved road, so the ride is bumpy. In return, coconut groves, fields and the sea alternate along the roadside, and the drive itself becomes a highlight. Plan your day around sunset time, and if driving back on a dark road feels like too much, stay a night at a beachfront bungalow or resort.

It is a good addition to a wider Tablas Island trip. Waterfalls and beaches cluster around San Andres and Odiongan in the north, and pairing the point with the Looc Marine Sanctuary in the south makes a full day. You can also link it with the morning boat from Carabao Island for an island-hopping itinerary. Public transport is almost nonexistent, so a motorbike or scooter is effectively the default way to get around.

The beach opens to the west, so you can watch the sun reach the horizon all the way down. Arrive about an hour before sunset to claim a good spot. The view is especially crisp in the dry season when clouds are few.
On calm evenings the sky and the palms reflect on the water. It is the photo spot visitors mention most. At low tide, the wet sand can also hold reflections.

Inside the beach there is a clearing lined with palms where you can sit in the shade. If the area right at the point is crowded, park at the clearing a little before it and walk. Many visitors also park their motorbikes directly on the sand.
Small boats pulled onto the sand, fishing nets and simple huts show everyday village life. When taking photos, ask permission before photographing people and fishing gear.
The beach, run by a local landowner, has huts, hammocks and a volleyball net, and sells Filipino food and cold drinks. A beachfront bungalow has been reported at about
per night. Check facilities and rates locally.

Nearby in Agmanic is a resort with cabins and safari-tent rooms where you can watch the sunset from the terrace. It is known to have a restaurant, a small set of gym equipment, and snorkeling and volleyball in front of the beach. Booking ahead is safer.

The last stretch has no paving, with rocks and muddy slopes that keep your speed down. There is pleasure in passing coconut plantations, fields and shoreline slowly. It suits riders with motorbike experience.
Rent a scooter in Looc or Odiongan and fill the tank. A scooter is reported at about

Before the final unpaved section, check your fuel and your motorbike headlight. The road is rough, so ride slowly.
Arrive at the beach, pay the
entrance fee and pick a spot. Start with the palm clearing and the boats on the sand.
Enjoy the sunset. Sunset time changes with the season, so check the time for the day you go.
Leave promptly before it gets dark. The road takes much longer in the dark.
The road back after dark is long and unlit. If you are not a confident driver, choose the one-night itinerary below instead of this one.

to reach Santa Fe port.
Find a scooter or a habal-habal (motorbike taxi) in Santa Fe. Asking your accommodation about transport in advance makes it easier.
Look around the nearby Santa Fe beaches and Canyayo Beach. Check the road and conditions locally before going.
Check in at Tablas Point and have lunch. Bring any snacks and water you need in advance.
Head to the beach and wait for the west-facing sunset. You can also watch it from a bungalow terrace.
Have dinner and rest early. The road tomorrow is long, so save your energy.
The next morning, stroll the beach, swim in the cool sea at sunrise, and then head back.

Small aircraft fly from Manila to Tugdan Airport (TBH) in Alcantara on Tablas Island. Operators and days change from year to year and flights are only a few per week, so check the latest schedule before booking.
One traveler reported about
1 hour 30 minutes
by road from the airport to Tablas Point. About three quarters of it is paved coastal road, and the last few kilometers are unpaved.
You can find a habal-habal outside the airport or ask the resort about pickup. Because flights are infrequent, it is best to fix your return date first.
Flights change often, so check the latest announcements.

From Santa Fe port, continue to the point by motorbike or local transport. Some resorts can arrange a boat pickup from Caticlan.

For an island-hopping trip, we recommend linking it with Carabao Island. Sailings can be cancelled by weather and waves, so confirm the day before.

Scooter rental is about
per day and fuel is about

A 15-minute tricycle or habal-habal ride costs about
, but longer rides need bargaining. There is almost no public transport to the point.
Tablas Island is warm all year, but for sunsets the dry season with fewer clouds is best. Santa Fe has average daytime highs of about
and nights of about
, with annual rainfall of about 1,264 mm.

Travel blogs call April to July the best weather and also peak season, November to March a decent period with short showers, and August to October typhoon season to avoid. The unpaved road turns to mud in the rain, so allow more travel time right after wet weather.

The beach at Tablas Point is reported to have huts, hammocks and a volleyball net set up by a local landowner, selling Filipino home cooking and cold drinks. A beachfront bungalow has been reported at about
per night, the simplest choice if you want both the sunset and the morning sea. Rooms, rates and menus can change, so check locally before you go.

Tablas Point Resort in Agmanic offers cabins and safari-tent rooms, runs a restaurant, and is known to offer snorkeling and volleyball in front of the beach. There are almost no shops nearby, so bring water, snacks, mosquito repellent and a power bank. More lodging and restaurants are in Odiongan, Looc and San Agustin, so on a day trip it is safer to eat there before or after.
Arrive an hour before sunset to claim a good spot. If the point itself is crowded, the palm clearing a little before it is also good.
Check your headlight, brakes and fuel before setting out. The last stretch is rocky, so slow down.
The road back at night is long and dark. If driving worries you, stay a night at a bungalow or resort.
Bring enough water, snacks and cash. In such a remote area, currency exchange and cash withdrawals are hard to find and many places do not take cards.
Right after rain the unpaved section becomes muddy. Adjust your plans to the weather.
Protect your camera and phone from sand and sea wind. A waterproof pouch helps.
Ask permission before photographing residents and fishing gear. Carry out all of your trash.
Boats, flights and entrance fees change. Before you leave, check the latest announcements with the Romblon tourism office or your accommodation.
The last stretch is unpaved, and the road back after sunset is dark and long. If you are not used to riding a motorbike or have no headlight, avoid traveling at night.
Signal is weak in many spots, so maps and contact can drop out. Download offline maps beforehand.
In typhoon season (August to October) boats stop and the road turns to mud, so leave extra time in your schedule.
Ask locals about currents and depth before swimming in the sea. There are almost no rescue facilities.
Flights to Tablas Island are infrequent, so if your return date slips the rest of your plans can unravel.
